en: The Treasury of Caryā Songs: Introduction 1.
Homage to the Innate (Sahaja)
It is far from being a positive entity, yet it is not even near to being a non-entity; it is beyond perception, neither past nor present, and though existing, it is not an object for the worlds.
It is the absence of nihilism, the Void, the sole refuge of all self-restrained ascetics.
Victorious is the single reality, the innate [nature] here in the form of the excellent Sugata. || 1 ||
2. The Sandhyābhāṣā Vandanā: Indeed, the Sandhyā language prevails here, in which the Siddhas proclaim the reality of the ultimate truth.
By making known the primacy of meaning,
they destroy any misplaced pride in the mere word.
Āgati is said to be sprinkling;
kṛpīṭa is considered to be a hand-drum (ḍamaruka); and abhavya is to be known as a frog (durdura).
Kāliñjara is considered to be auspicious. || 3 ||
The drum is said to be "touchless," the skull is the lotus vessel,
and the food should be known as that which brings satisfaction.
The condiment is jasmine fuel. || 4 ||
Feces is said to be equal to the four [fragrant substances], urine is remembered as musk,
and self-arisen [substance] is to be known as frankincense.
Śukra is considered to be camphor;
mahāmāṃsa is said to be the bee; and the union of the two organs is kunduru.
The vajra is known as the *bola*,
and the lotus is considered to be the *kakkolaka*.
The family is known to be fivefold, distinguished by the division of castes; these are the sandhyābhāṣās, and the Buddhas are the five Kaulikas.
The Ḍombī is renowned as belonging to the Vajra family, the Naṭī likewise to the Padma family, the Śvapacī to the Ratna family, and the Dvijā is considered to belong to the Tathāgata family. (8)
The washerwoman and the woman of the artisan caste—these mudrās bestow excellent siddhi.
Their semen is the vajra; having worshipped it, the observer of the vow should drink it.
O Vajragarbha, Great Being, whatever has been spoken by me to you—all that should be respectfully grasped as the most wonderful intentional language (*sandhyābhāṣa*). (10)
Whoever who has been consecrated here does not speak in the twilight language (saṃdhyābhāṣā), an offense against the equality [of the community] occurs for him; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, even if he has awakened, he dies from calamities, thieves, and the fevers of the planets, if— even though he is enlightened— he does not speak the intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*).
If one does not speak these words after having approached those who know their own samaya,
then the yoginīs born of the four seats (catuṣpīṭha) will cause agitation.

Having thus taught in the third chapter, titled "The Sandhyā-bhāṣā of the Nidāna of All Tantras," the Blessed One spoke again in the fourth chapter, titled "The Summary Meaning" (Piṇḍārtha): "In Kolla resides Bolā; in Mummuṇi is Kakkolā. When the clouds thunder with a harsh sound, Karuṇā comes with a cry of 'Aina-rolā'. (1)
In old age, *bola* abides in silence; in profound silence, *kakkola*. O, the skin-sound of the compassionate one is played as wealth by the *kṛpoṭa*.
There, they eat food at will and drink intense wine;
having taken refuge in that unswerving compassion, they perform the salutation of the Siddhas.
Leading people to the fulfillment of their purpose through wisdom,
those perfected ones who are skilled in the ultimate truth— untainted by the world through the power of emptiness— truly triumph. (3)
4. Homage to the Eighty-four Siddhas:
I pay homage to the eighty-four Siddhas who consist of the knowledge of yoga;
though born from all castes and families, they have reached the ultimate state beyond caste.
5. Salutation to the external Siddhas known as Nātha:

for those whose minds perceive the Lords as possessing attributes, there is always [salutation] to the Lords who are indeed devoid of attributes; yet for those whose state of mind is that of being without a protector, there is always [salutation] to those who possess attributes, for they bring about the end of the notion of being without a protector.

[This is] eternally for those who dwell in the external ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) through trivial meditations (dhāraṇā), and eternally for those who sport in yoga and the perfections of yoga (yogasiddhi).
Constantly devoted to the refutation of the doctrine of birth,
and constantly observing the vow of mental application toward the Protector,
they have forever established the path of the Buddhist Siddhas together with Īśvara.
I perpetually bow at the feet of those who do not wander among the classes of birth.

6. Having performed the salutation to Śānta, which is headed by devotion to Rāma and includes Īśa, he follows the path of Nātha with a practice of yoga that is minimal, because the qualities of the path of Yoga have become subordinate.
Having determined Rāma to be devoid of attributes, having set aside Rāma as possessing attributes,
and having brought to mind the innate Rāma from the perspective of the Buddha-body;

Victorious on earth are those saints known by the name of Kabīr, who have subdued the intoxication of birth with the stream of devotion to Rāma, and who have spread compassion throughout their minds as the essence of all things.
I bow with great reverence at their feet day after day.

I bow to the Speech that is peaceful, free from all faults, and present here within the bodies of all beings; I praise that Speech which eternally teaches great patience among the multitudes of sentient beings.
She who always teaches the Dharma centered on great compassion,
which indeed keeps all forms of violence at a distance and is difficult to transgress.
Endowed with wisdom joined with the means for the true goal, she brings about purposeful activity that is certainly unsurpassed;
she proclaims the boundless benefits of peace in its infinite qualities.
The supreme authority, comparable to the attainment of the immeasurable.
Furthermore, in the context of defining the innate reality (*sahajatattva*), there is the homage to the innate:
that which the Sugata experienced as ineffable, and that very thing which he taught as ineffable.
May that very [reality], which has been extensively elaborated upon in all the scriptures, shine forth to me with its syllables perfectly offered.

9. The secret nature of the Innate and its dependence on the authority of the Guru is as follows: just as a young girl hears of sexual union from the mouth of her friend, though it is beyond the range of words and syllables.
In the same way, a virtuous person receives from the mouth of the Guru that which is innate to one who understands it through the ear. || 9 ||
10. One experiences the innate (sahaja) within one's own body; whether staying at home or dwelling in solitude, having relied upon the Guru, one should apply oneself with effort to yoga.
Within his own body, he brings about great bliss;
through that bliss, the various [states] arisen for the virtuous are directly realized. || 10 ||
11. Just as Mount Sumeru, the abode of many divine beings, beautifies the lakes, rivers, and clusters of lotuses, so too is there a thorough understanding of the body.
In the very same way, the assembly of channels and the rotation of the wheels remain supported by the Jina, like the central axis of Mount Meru. || 11 ||
Below the spinal column, in the region supported by the rectum,
resides the first wheel, known by the name Sukhapāla.
At the navel, heart, throat, and head, there are four wheels on Mount Meru,
known respectively as Nirmāṇa, Dharma, Saṃbhoga, and Mahāsukha.
In these four wheels of the elements, the Jina known as Sahaja abides as the field of accomplishment for the Siddhas, consisting of the four bodies. || 14 ||
Just as the channels (nāḍīs) exist within the bodies of the Victors, so too is there an entry;
she is renowned as Avadhūtī, having made her abode in the Meru of the body. 15.
On both sides of this [central channel], two other channels remain;
therefore, this central one is the "first lunar day" (pratipadā), which leads to the Victor. || 16 ||
The lalanā channel, the lunar duct, is to be observed on the left nostril;
the rasanā channel, the solar duct, is on the right. (17)
In this body there are many channels that are turned away from the ultimate goal; however, there is but one, the Middle Way, which leads to the true goal and is beloved by the Sugata. (18)
In this body of men, there is likewise this network of channels, which takes its support just as a lotus stalk and flower do within a pond. (19)
The conception of lotus petals and stalks within the wheels that resemble lotuses was taught by the perfected ones who know the meaning of reality, in order to meditate upon that reality. (20)

12. The Convention of the Means of Accomplishment: Even from the non-emission of the *bodhicitta* during the union of the jewel and the lotus, and from the union of the vowels and consonants (*āli-kāli*), and from the cessation of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). || 21 ||
For those who dwell in the field of the Victors by means of the path of the *avadhūtī* alone, there is a constant abiding of the mind here in the empty, great bliss that is full. (22)

This is the resting of the mind, the teaching on the goal for the perfected ones; it is the state in which the movement of the mind devoid of vital breath ceases, producing neither cold nor heat. (23)
When the innate is made manifest, this is union with the Buddha; this dharma is "come and see," the personal domain of the virtuous. (24)
That state of the mind remaining unshakable in bliss, having opened the path of the *avadhūtī* with effort— that,
in truth, is the manifestation of the innate (*sahaja*).
And that very same [union] is the union with the Caṇḍālikā. || 25 ||
For those who possess the attainment of the two-in-two, there is no falling away from the nectar-water of the conventional mind of awakening;
in that very body, there is the attainment of the seal (mudrā) with exceeding joy.
This secret is thus within this casket.
The momentary, the variegated, the ripening, the momentary, the momentary destruction, and thereafter the dissimilar;
thus they delight in the fourfold set of moments.
Having encountered each pair, the virtuous become [perfected]. || 27 ||
In one moment there is manifold external pleasure; in another moment, at its ripening, there is the sensation of bliss;
in yet another moment, it is fully established as the bliss of liberation.
That which is non-conceptual and momentary is devoid of defining characteristics.
For all this— whether it be innate or higher and lower, transcendent in form or that which possesses form— is indeed that very [reality];
how then could those traveling the path to accomplishment ever [perceive it otherwise]?
Indeed, they become intoxicated at the moment of union with the Kunduru. || 29 ||
The spray of bliss here brings a distinct satisfaction, like a great ocean compared to the Great Bliss;
however, that supreme reality itself is not found therein.
Therefore, until death, one should take only a portion of that as the ultimate reality.
That great bliss, when not conceptualized by the mind,
is such that the movement of the sun and the lord of the night cannot proceed.
There is no access there for those possessed by passion; it is for those free from passion. || 31 ||
That which is stainless, innate, free from duality, great bliss, equal to space, and indeed without mind;
it is equal in flavor, the non-mental engagement that is the fruit of reality.
The Tathāgata is that ultimate cessation. || 32 ||
It may be made of gold or even of iron;
the shackle binds and does not release. It may indeed have a real purpose or even a false one.
An imagined object is not said to be the ultimate reality. || 32 ||
The mind does not operate upon an object that is not conceptually constructed;
how, then, could wretched speech operate?
Therefore, those who maintain silence are supreme in the teaching of the ultimate truth.
Thus do the Tathāgatas become partakers of the state of a Sage. || 34 ||

That reality is neither empty nor, again, non-empty; it shines forth as active, yet it does not proceed by following after existence or non-existence. It is of equal flavor, forever shaken free from the nets of conceptual constructions.
It is not an object of either the eye or the mind, whether in the presence of the senses or out of their sight. || 35 ||
In this world, people constantly recite and meditate upon the reality known as the Nameless through various nets of names belonging to the gods in their diverse forms,
employing numerous scriptural collections consisting of many words.
For it is only those of dull intellect who, being ignorant, openly approach [the Lord]. || 36 ||
That one God alone is always to be beheld through the methods of hearing, reflection, and meditation by means of the entire multitude of scriptures with their many branches;
Him alone do the sons of the Sugata and the hosts of perfected ones [behold] as one who delights in the Self.
Beholding them in their bodies as they move about here in this world, those of meritorious deeds [are seen]. || 37 ||
This innate state is difficult to attain; only a rare person hears of it, and indeed,
even rarer is one who strives through its practice.
But he who attains it is indeed rare to find. || 38 ||
Entering into this supreme secret even within the secret,
those born from the essence of the Jina joyfully sing this through their own conduct.
They were intoxicated by the nectar of beautiful songs and dohās. || 39 ||
These words here attain supreme purity, resembling sacred mantras in their profundity;
they are always to be understood by those who know the secret Vedas.
Who among people here knows [this] in its entirety? || 40 ||
13. Recollection of the spiritual friend: so that the meaning of words may become clear according to their literal sense, one becomes capable of penetrating the intended meaning.
Thus, observing the words of Prabodhacandra, I applied myself with diligent effort. || 41 ||
While the text was being purified, annotated, and clarified simultaneously according to the occasion,
it so happened that this work was printed here in only a small portion.
"Leaving us behind, Prabodha has gone there to heaven. || 42 ||
On the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, at the final moment of Wednesday, before the commencement of Thursday and prior to the setting of the sun. (43)
When the world was languid and the Leader of the World had passed into nirvāṇa,
[there arose] one whose eyes were the unique sky of the dual [moon and sun].
In the year of Vikramārka. || 44 ||
The illustrious Prabodhacandra, the joy of the Bāgacī lineage, attained peace in his final moments even as we were looking on. (45)
Upon this absolute separation from her, his mind became paralyzed;
he beheld the quarters as empty, for darkness pervaded everything on all sides.
Moreover, in this state, through the recollection of its merit and with great effort, the text has been purified by means of annotations just as before. (47)
Having examined his works according to the prescribed method, and also by means of my own reasoning to the best of my intellectual capacity, [I have composed this]. (48)
Whatever ill-deeds were done here, let them all belong to me, the one of small intellect;
for whatever well-deeds were done, let them all belong to that one of great wisdom. (49)
I bow to him of the most noble mind, whose virtuous fame is celebrated;
for he is remembered incessantly here as if with nectar.
In this world, he alone is worthy of honor among men whose mouth is filled with discourse on the face of every person;
he by whom the firm seed of the method of purification has been sown here through knowledge.
I bow with devotion here to that friend who has gone to heaven. || 51 ||
To the sovereign lord of speech, possessed of noble discernment,
whose mind is intent on the realization of knowledge, who possesses a gentle heart,
and who is accompanied by a host of excellent disciples and fellow practitioners.
For I have been purchased by your virtues; here I bow before you.
Seeing the moon has set, the people become anxious, waiting for the untimely dawn;
yet when this moon, their dearest friend, has departed forever, they remain as they were.
"How indeed could it be maintained by me in this great darkness? (53)
Your name is nectar to be licked by the tongue;
indeed, the play of your speech is a treasury for remembering it.
You are the entire manuscript, the worthy recipient of all study.
You are not he, yet by your form you are here always worthy of salutation.
The Jina teaches that the entire world is indeed empty; everyone here reaches emptiness through the power of time. For the benefit of the world, the Buddhas manifest bodies in this realm.
But having passed that time, they were not able to seize him. 55.
That emptiness which strips away the pale leaves in the forest, which causes new sprouts to produce tender foliage,
and without which there is indeed no movement within the phenomenal world.
Victorious is she, the sovereign of all, who has transcended the phenomenal world.
I bow to that Tathāgata, the King of Emptiness, the monk Śānti, for whom great compassion and emptiness are the auspicious foundation of his teaching. (57)
